question: Two aircraft converge at approximately the same level. The other aircraft is on your right. Who gives way?

options.B: The one at the lower altitude

explanation: the aircraft that has the other on its right gives way.

question: Two aircraft approach head-on with risk of collision. Action?
explanation: both alter heading to the right.

question: "Overtaking" means approaching another aircraft from behind at an angle of less than…
explanation: less than 70° to the plane of symmetry of the aircraft being overtaken (at night, you'd see only its rear white light).

question: An overtaking aircraft must:

options.D: Alter heading to the right and stay clear

explanation: the overtaken aircraft has right of way; the overtaker goes right and keeps clear until well past.

question: A power-driven aeroplane must give way to:
explanation: powered heavier-than-air aircraft give way to airships, gliders and balloons.

question: Which aircraft has priority over the others in converging situations?

options.B: An aeroplane towing another aircraft or object

explanation: all aircraft give way to those towing. (Balloons have priority over gliders, not "everything".)

question: Two aircraft approach to land. Who has right of way?

options.A: The one further from the runway

explanation: the lower aircraft, but it must not cut in front of another already on final, nor overtake it.

question: You know another aircraft is compelled to land (emergency). You should:
explanation: aircraft aware another is compelled to land shall give way.

question: Two aircraft taxiing head-on. Correct action?

options.A: Both stop or turn right where practicable
options.D: The one with power on goes first

explanation: On the ground head-on: each stops or turns right if practicable. Same 'keep right' logic as in the air.

question: A taxiing aircraft and an aircraft taking off. Who gives way?
explanation: taxiing aircraft gives way to aircraft taking off or about to.

question: Minimum height for VFR flight elsewhere than over congested areas (not taking off/landing)?

options.B: 150 m (500 ft) above ground or water

explanation: SERA.5005; and always able to land without undue hazard in case of engine failure.

question: Minimum height over congested areas (city/town/assembly)?

options.B: 1000 ft (300 m) above the highest obstacle within 600 m radius

explanation: Congested areas need more margin (1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m) so an engine failure doesn't force a landing on people or buildings. Example: 200 ft tower → fly ≥1200 ft above ground.

question: Aerodrome circuits: unless otherwise published, turns are made to the…
explanation: left, unless a right-hand circuit is published (LKBE publishes right-hand for RWY 24/27!).

question: Take-off and landing should normally be made:
explanation: unless safety, runway configuration or traffic dictate otherwise.

question: Light gun — steady green to an aircraft in flight means:
explanation: Steady green in flight = cleared to land. Memory: green = go. Flashing green means 'return for landing', not yet cleared.

question: Light gun — steady red to an aircraft in flight:

options.B: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling

explanation: Steady red in flight = give way and keep circling; you are not cleared. Don't confuse with flashing red (aerodrome unsafe).

question: Light gun — flashing red in flight:
explanation: Flashing red in flight = aerodrome unsafe, do not land. Steady red only means give way and continue circling.

question: Light gun — flashing green in flight:
explanation: return for landing, to be followed by steady green.

question: Light gun — steady green to an aircraft on the ground:
explanation: (flashing green = cleared to taxi).

question: Light gun — flashing red on the ground:

options.C: Taxi clear of the landing area in use

explanation: (steady red = stop).

question: Light gun — flashing white on the ground:

options.D: Return to starting point on the aerodrome

explanation: Flashing white on the ground = return to the starting point on the aerodrome. It is the only white signal in the gun code.

question: You are intercepted; the interceptor rocks its wings. It means:

options.A: You have been intercepted — follow me

explanation: acknowledge by rocking wings, follow, try 121.5, squawk 7700 if no other instruction.

question: Transponder code for unlawful interference (hijack):
explanation: 7500 = unlawful interference (hijack). Memory: 75 'seventy-five' — 'Hi-jack, five-oh'. Only squawk it if safe to do so.

question: Transponder code for radio communication failure:
explanation: 7600 = radio failure. Memory: '76' — 'six-o-o... nothing heard'. ATC then expects you to follow lost-comms procedures.

question: Transponder code for general emergency:
explanation: 7700 = general emergency (Mayday). Memory: 77 = 'Heaven'. Use with a MAYDAY/PAN call.

question: Navigation lights: which is correct (aircraft viewed from above)?

options.A: Left red, right green, tail white
options.B: Left green, right red, tail white

explanation: red port, green starboard, white tail.

question: Speed limit for VFR below FL100 in the Czech Republic (Class C–G)?
explanation: 250 kt IAS below FL100 applies to VFR in the CZ (Classes C–G). Light trainers never approach it, but it is a classic exam number.

question: Aviation time reference is:
explanation: UTC (Czech local = UTC+1, +2 in summer time).

question: A white dumb-bell on the signal square means:

options.A: Aircraft to use runways and taxiways only

explanation: A white dumb-bell means movement is restricted to runways and taxiways only (usually because of soft grass). Look at the signal square before taxiing.

question: A red square with yellow diagonals crossing (X) on the signal square means:
explanation: Red square with yellow crossing diagonals = landing prohibited. A single yellow diagonal means 'special precautions'.

question: SERA is:

options.C: Standardised European Rules of the Air

explanation: Regulation (EU) 923/2012.

question: ICAO Annex 2 covers:
explanation: (Annex 1 licensing, 14 aerodromes, 13 accident investigation, 11 ATS).

question: ICAO Annex 1 covers:
explanation: Annex 1 = personnel licensing. Memory: 1 = 'One licence per pilot'. Annex 2 = rules of the air; 14 = aerodromes; 13 = accident investigation.

question: ICAO Annex 13 covers:
explanation: Annex 13 = accident and incident investigation. 13 = 'unlucky thirteen'.

question: ICAO Annex 14 covers:
explanation: (Annex 11 = air traffic services).

question: Which airspace classes exist in the Czech Republic?

options.B: A, B, C, D, E, G

explanation: The CR uses only four classes: C, D, E, G (no A, B or F). Controlled = C, D, E; uncontrolled = G.

question: Class C in the Czech Republic is:

options.C: TMA Praha and CTA2 Praha above FL95

explanation: Prague TMA is the only TMA in Class C; other CTR/TMA are Class D.

question: Class G in the CR extends:
explanation: Class G runs from the ground to 1000 ft AGL outside a CTR. Above that it is Class E up to FL95.

question: Class E in the CR (outside CTR/TMA):

options.C: Above 1000 ft AGL up to FL95

explanation: Class E starts at 1000 ft AGL (outside CTR/TMA) and goes to FL95. Being 'E' means controlled airspace, but VFR needs no clearance.

question: VFR flight in Class E requires:
explanation: In Class E VFR needs neither clearance nor radio, but you still get traffic info 'as far as practicable'. Class D and C need both.

question: VFR flight in Class D requires:

options.B: ATC clearance and continuous two-way radio

explanation: Class D: clearance + continuous two-way radio, but ATC only gives traffic information (no VFR separation).

question: In Class C, ATC separates VFR traffic from:
explanation: VFR receives traffic information on other VFR.

question: Service provided in Class G:
explanation: Class G = uncontrolled: Flight Information Service and Alerting only. No separation, no clearance.

question: VMC in Class E below FL100 (Czech Republic)?

options.B: 5 km, 1500 m horizontally / 1000 ft vertically from cloud

explanation: Class E VMC below FL100: 5 km, 1500 m horizontal / 1000 ft vertical from cloud. Remember '5-1500-1000'.

question: VMC visibility at/above FL100 in Class C/D/E?
explanation: At or above FL100 the visibility requirement rises to 8 km (faster aircraft need more time to see and avoid).

question: Class G at/below 3000 ft AMSL (Czech VFR Manual) minimum:

options.B: 1500 m, clear of cloud, in sight of surface

explanation: with speed ≤140 kt IAS allowing reduction to 1500 m.

question: Class G above 3000 ft AMSL minimum:

options.B: 5 km, 1500 m horizontally / 1000 ft vertically from cloud

explanation: Above 3000 ft AMSL in Class G, minima are 5 km and 1500 m/1000 ft from cloud (the same as Class E).

question: LKBE elevation 1322 ft; circuit altitude 2460 ft AMSL. The circuit is flown in Class:
explanation: 2460 − 1322 = 1138 ft AGL, above the 1000 ft AGL Class G ceiling.

question: A Radio Mandatory Zone (RMZ) requires:

options.B: Radio equipment carried and operated; initial call before entry

explanation: RMZ: radio must be carried and operated, with an initial call (callsign, type, position, level, intentions) before entry. No clearance implied.

question: A Transponder Mandatory Zone (TMZ) requires:

options.B: Operating SSR transponder with altitude reporting

explanation: TMZ: a working SSR transponder with altitude reporting is mandatory. Radio is a separate requirement (RMZ).

question: Prohibited areas in the CR are prefixed:
explanation: LKP prohibited, LKR restricted, LKD danger.

question: Danger area prefix:
explanation: Danger area = LKD (D for Danger). Prohibited = LKP, Restricted = LKR.

question: Restricted area prefix:
explanation: Restricted = LKR (R for Restricted). Entry only under conditions published for that area.

question: Entry to a Danger area is:

options.B: Not formally prohibited; hazardous activity may occur — PIC judgement

explanation: Danger areas are not forbidden, but hazardous activity may happen at published times. The PIC judges the risk; best practice: avoid.

question: A TSA (Temporary Segregated Area) means:

options.A: Exclusive use — no transit while active

explanation: (TRA: transit may be possible with clearance).

question: A "TRA GA" while activated:
explanation: While a TRA GA is active it becomes Class G so uncontrolled circuit/glider flying can happen near a controlled aerodrome.

question: How long is activation info on a TSA/TRA valid once obtained?
explanation: after that, re-check or assume active.

question: Standard ATZ dimensions (no local exception):
explanation: Standard ATZ: 3 NM radius from the ARP, up to 4000 ft, unless the AIP says otherwise.

question: LKBE frequency:
explanation: LKBE = Bene Radio 118.005 (information only, not control). Memorise it with the callsign.

question: LKBE circuit directions for powered aircraft:
explanation: gliders fly the opposite hand.

question: LKBE take-off on RWY 09L/R is allowed:

options.D: Only with approval of the information unit

explanation: then turn left heading 045° to avoid villages.

question: LKBE ATZ village-avoidance rule:

options.B: Stay 300 m from villages or fly ≥2953 ft (900 m) AMSL

explanation: Inside the LKBE ATZ either stay ≥300 m from villages or fly at or above 2953 ft (900 m) AMSL — protects villagers from low flying.

question: Which LKBE runways are night-VFR usable (with lighting and prior agreement)?
explanation: using TWY C.

question: LKBE is:
explanation: you are never "cleared"; you remain responsible for separation.

question: Does LKBE have a published METAR?
explanation: No METAR at LKBE; Prague-Kbely (~43 km) is too far to represent local weather. Ask the operator and use your own eyes.

question: What is the Class of airspace above 1000 ft AGL at Benešov outside CTR/TMA?
explanation: LKBE is outside any CTR/TMA: above 1000 ft AGL is Class E. Ground level up to 1000 ft AGL is G.

question: A CTR is:

options.B: Airspace from surface to a specified upper limit around an aerodrome for controlled IFR flights

explanation: A CTR (control zone) protects arrivals/departures near an aerodrome, from the surface up to a stated limit.

question: A TMA is generally:

options.B: Controlled airspace at the confluence of ATS routes near major aerodromes

explanation: A TMA is controlled airspace around major aerodromes where ATS routes converge, usually starting above a CTR.

question: Class D VMC minima are the same as which?
explanation: Class D VMC minima equal Class C minima; the difference is the service (C separates VFR from IFR, D gives only traffic info).

question: What does the "Class E" designation give a VFR pilot?

options.D: Traffic information as far as practicable, no separation

explanation: In Class E, VFR gets traffic information as far as practicable, no separation. See-and-avoid is entirely yours.

question: An FI certificate is valid for:
To revalidate an FI certificate you must meet:
explanation: (a) 50 h instruction incl. 15 h in last 12 months; (b) instructor refresher seminar; (c) assessment of competence.

question: Revalidation condition (a) requires:

options.B: 50 h instruction, of which 15 h in the 12 months before expiry

explanation: Revalidation option (a): 50 h of instruction in the validity period, of which 15 h in the last 12 months. The 15 h recency prevents a 'front-loaded' claim.

question: For every second revalidation:
explanation: Every second revalidation must include the assessment of competence — you cannot use only hours/seminar twice in a row.

question: To renew a lapsed FI certificate:

options.C: Refresher seminar AND assessment of competence, in the 12 months before renewal

explanation: Renewal after lapse needs a refresher seminar AND an assessment of competence, both within 12 months before renewal.

question: Minimum total flight time to start an FI(A) course (CPL holder):
explanation: FI(A) entry: 200 h total incl. 150 h PIC (CPL route). This is why the check-ride/pre-entry test matters.

question: Prior SEP experience needed for FI(A):

options.B: 30 h on SEP aeroplanes, incl. 5 h in the 6 months before the pre-entry flight test

explanation: 30 h on SEP aeroplanes with 5 h in the previous 6 months. If your SEP hours are older, fly before the test.

question: Instrument flight instruction required before the FI(A) course:

options.B: 10 h, of which no more than 5 in an FSTD

explanation: 10 h of instrument instruction (max 5 in an FSTD) — the rest must be in an aeroplane.

question: Cross-country requirement for FI(A) entry:

options.A: 20 h PIC, incl. a 300 NM flight with two full-stop landings at two different aerodromes

explanation: 20 h cross-country as PIC including a 300 NM flight with two full-stop landings at two different aerodromes.

question: The pre-entry flight test must be completed within:
explanation: and is based on the class-rating proficiency check (Appendix 9). *Your F AIR check ride is effectively this test.*

question: A newly qualified (restricted) FI must:

options.B: Instruct only under supervision until 100 h instruction and 25 student solos
options.D: Only fly with a CPL student

explanation: A restricted FI works under supervision until 100 h of instruction and 25 student solos have been completed.

question: A restricted FI:

options.D: May not authorise student solo flights independently

explanation: supervising FI nominated by the ATO must authorise.

question: Hours of flight instruction needed to lift the restriction:
explanation: (plus supervising at least 25 student solo flights).

question: FI(A) privileges include instruction for:

options.A: PPL(A) and class ratings for single-pilot SE aeroplanes

explanation: CPL/IR/MEP/FI instruction needs extra experience/qualification.

question: To instruct for the CPL(A), an FI needs at least:

options.B: 500 h flight time incl. 200 h flight instruction

explanation: CPL instruction needs 500 h flight time including 200 h of flight instruction — a high bar that you build over years.

question: Recent experience to carry passengers (FCL.060):

options.A: 3 take-offs, approaches and landings in the previous 90 days on same type/class

explanation: FCL.060: 3 take-offs, approaches and landings in the previous 90 days (same type/class) to carry passengers.

question: Night passenger carriage requires (without IR):

options.A: At least 1 of the 3 take-offs/landings performed at night

explanation: Night passengers: at least one of those three landings at night, unless you hold an IR.

question: English language proficiency Level 4 is valid for:
explanation: Level 5 = 6 years; Level 6 = unlimited.

question: SEP class rating validity:
explanation: SEP class rating lasts 2 years. Revalidate by experience or proficiency check in the window before expiry.

question: SEP revalidation by experience (in the 12 months before expiry):

options.A: 12 h flight time incl. 6 h PIC, 12 take-offs/landings, and 1 h refresher training with an FI/CRI

explanation: alternatively a proficiency check in the 3 months before expiry.

question: Class 1 medical validity for a pilot under 40 (commercial single-pilot, no passengers-over-60 restriction):
explanation: 6 months if 40+ (and for single-pilot CAT with passengers over 60).

question: Class 2 medical validity for a pilot under 40:
explanation: 24 months for 40–50; 12 months over 50.

question: Minimum age for PPL / CPL:
explanation: solo from 16.

question: Which organisation type is required to run an FI course?
explanation: DTOs are limited to PPL/LAPL-level training.

question: A DTO differs from an ATO because it:

options.D: Declares activity to the CAA instead of being approved

explanation: A DTO only declares its activity to the authority; an ATO is approved. FI courses need an ATO.

question: Theoretical knowledge exam credit for CPL: pass all within a period, then valid for licence issue for:
explanation: pass all subjects within 18 months / 6 sittings; valid 36 months.

question: Minimum total flight time for a CPL (non-integrated):
explanation: (integrated course: 150 h).

question: Who issues your licence?

options.A: The competent authority of the Member State

explanation: Licences are issued by the competent authority of the Member State (in Czechia, ÚCL), not by EASA.

question: A student pilot may fly solo after:

options.A: Instructor authorisation of first solo, per the approved training programme

explanation: First solo is authorised by the instructor under the approved training programme, not by a fixed hour count.

question: For instructor duties in a training flight the FI is:

options.A: PIC unless agreed otherwise (instructor responsible for safe conduct)

explanation: On instructional flights the instructor is PIC unless clearly agreed otherwise, and remains responsible for safety.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Maximum flight time in a calendar year (ORO.FTL.210):
explanation: ORO.FTL: 900 h flight time in a calendar year. Memory: 900 / 100 / 1000.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Maximum flight time in 28 consecutive days:
explanation: 100 h flight time in any 28 consecutive days. Memory: 900 / 100 / 1000.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Maximum flight time in 12 consecutive calendar months:
explanation: 1000 h in 12 consecutive calendar months. Memory: 900 / 100 / 1000.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Maximum duty hours in 7 consecutive days:
explanation: Duty: 60 h in any 7 days. Memory: 60 / 110 / 190.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Maximum duty hours in 14 consecutive days:
explanation: Duty: 110 h in any 14 days. Memory: 60 / 110 / 190.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Maximum duty hours in 28 consecutive days:
explanation: Duty: 190 h in any 28 days. Memory: 60 / 110 / 190.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: "Flight time" (block-to-block) is measured from:

options.D: When the aircraft first moves to take off until it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight

explanation: Flight time is block-to-block: from first movement for take-off until the aircraft finally stops after landing.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: "Flying Duty Period (FDP)" begins when:

options.D: The pilot is required to report for duty that includes a sector or series of sectors

explanation: it ends when the aircraft comes to rest after the last sector.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: "Duty" means:

options.C: Any task carried out at the request of the operator (flying, admin, ground duties)

explanation: Duty covers any task done for the operator (flying, ground school, admin), not just flying.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Basic maximum daily FDP (acclimatised, start 06:00–13:29, 1–2 sectors):
explanation: Basic maximum daily FDP starts at 13 h for a 1–2 sector duty starting 06:00–13:29 (acclimatised).

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: For each sector beyond two, the basic maximum daily FDP is reduced by:
explanation: Each extra sector beyond two cuts the FDP by 30 min. 3 sectors → 12:30; 4 → 12:00.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: The commander may extend the maximum daily FDP at his discretion by up to:
explanation: only for unforeseen circumstances, with reporting to the operator.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Minimum rest at home base:

options.C: At least as long as the preceding duty period, or 12 h, whichever is greater

explanation: Home-base rest = longer of the preceding duty period or 12 h. Example: 10 h duty → 12 h rest; 14 h duty → 14 h rest.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Minimum rest away from home base:

options.B: At least as long as the preceding duty or 10 h, whichever is greater — including an 8 h sleep opportunity

explanation: Away from base: longer of preceding duty or 10 h, which must include an 8 h sleep opportunity.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Recurrent extended recovery rest must be at least:
explanation: Recurrent extended recovery rest = 36 h including two local nights.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: No more than … may elapse between the end of one recurrent extended recovery rest and the start of the next:
explanation: No more than 168 h (7 days) may pass between two recurrent extended recovery rests.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: A "local night" is:

options.B: 8 h period falling between 22:00 and 08:00 local time

explanation: A local night = 8 h between 22:00 and 08:00 local time.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: A crew member who feels unfit through fatigue must:

options.B: Not fly and inform the operator
options.D: Ask another crew member to hide it

explanation: fatigue is a fitness-to-fly issue (IMSAFE: F).

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: ORO.FTL formally applies to:
explanation: training organisations use their approved manual and national rules, benchmarked on EASA.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Which limit is the *tightest* for a busy instructor in a week?
explanation: 60 duty hours in 7 days is the tightest constraint for a busy instructor: 6 days × 10 h duty already reaches it.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: An instructor flies 4 sectors in one FDP starting 08:00. Basic max FDP?

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: After 10 h duty at home base the minimum rest is:
explanation: greater of duty length (10) or 12.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: After 15 h duty at home base the minimum rest is:
explanation: Rest must be at least as long as duty when duty exceeds 12 h: 15 h duty → 15 h rest.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Which is *not* a purpose of FTL rules?
explanation: FTL exists for fatigue management and safety, not for pay.

subtopic: Flight Time & Duty Limitations (EASA ORO.FTL benchmark)
question: Standard technique: to plan an instructor's roster you must monitor first:

options.B: Rolling 7/14/28-day duty and 28-day/12-month flight-time limits together

explanation: Monitor all rolling limits together (7/14/28-day duty and 28-day/12-month flight time); the tightest one binds first.

question: Instruments required for day VFR (NCO.IDE.A.120):

options.A: Magnetic heading, time (h/min/s), pressure altitude, IAS

explanation: Day VFR minimum: magnetic heading, time (h/min/s), pressure altitude, IAS. Memory: 'HATS' — Heading, Altitude, Time, Speed.

question: Seat belts/restraints are required for:
explanation: Restraints are needed for every occupant seat, not just the pilot's.

question: Which document proves the aircraft is registered?
explanation: Certificate of Registration proves nationality and owner. C of A proves airworthiness; ARC renews it.

question: Which document must be renewed regularly (typically annually) to keep the C of A valid?
explanation: The ARC (Airworthiness Review Certificate) is renewed annually to keep the aircraft legal.

question: ARROW stands for:

options.A: Airworthiness, Registration, Radio licence, Operating limitations, Weight & balance

explanation: ARROW: Airworthiness, Registration, Radio licence, Operating limitations (POH), Weight & balance.

question: Which is *not* required on board?
explanation: logbook isn't an aircraft document (licence and medical are required).

question: Minimum fuel for a day VFR flight (NCO.OP.125): destination plus:
explanation: 45 min for night; F AIR may require more.

question: An ELT (or PLB) is required to:

options.B: Help SAR find the aircraft after an accident

explanation: An ELT transmits on 121.5/406 MHz to help search and rescue locate the aircraft after an accident.

question: Life jackets are required when flying over water:

options.C: Beyond gliding distance from land (or as regulation specifies)

explanation: Life jackets are needed when flying beyond gliding distance from land over water, plus a risk assessment.

question: Who is responsible for checking weight & balance and fuel before flight?
explanation: The PIC is responsible for fuel, mass and balance and overall legality. You cannot delegate responsibility.

question: Airspeed indicator colour: white arc is:
explanation: bottom Vs0, top Vfe.

question: Green arc:
explanation: Green arc = normal range, from Vs1 to Vno.

question: Yellow arc:

options.B: Caution range — smooth air only (Vno to Vne)

explanation: Yellow arc = caution, Vno to Vne — smooth air only.

question: Red line is:
explanation: Red radial line = Vne, never exceed.

question: Vfe means:
explanation: Vfe = maximum speed with flaps extended. White arc top.

question: Va means:
explanation: full deflection below Va can't exceed load limits.

question: Vno means:

options.D: Max structural cruising speed — exceed only in smooth air

explanation: Vno = maximum structural cruising speed. Above it, only in smooth air. Top of the green arc.

question: Vne means:
explanation: Vne = never exceed speed; structural damage risk above it.

question: Vx gives:
explanation: obstacle clearance.

question: Vy gives:
explanation: Vy = best rate of climb (most height per minute). Vx = best angle (most height per distance, for obstacles).

question: Vs0 is stall speed:
explanation: Vs0 = stall speed in the landing configuration (flaps down). Bottom of the white arc.

question: Vs1 is stall speed:
explanation: Vs1 = stall speed in a specified configuration, usually clean. Bottom of the green arc.

question: Which document lists the aircraft's limitations and performance?
explanation: The AFM/POH lists limitations, procedures and performance. It must be on board.

question: The journey (technical) log records:

options.C: Flight and maintenance information such as flight times, defects, refuelling

explanation: The journey/technical log records flight times, defects, fuel and maintenance.

question: Before flight the PIC must ensure the aircraft:

options.A: Has valid documents and is airworthy and legal for the flight

explanation: The PIC must confirm documents, airworthiness and legality before flying.

question: The four-stroke cycle in order:
explanation: Induction → Compression → Power → Exhaust. Memory: 'Suck, squeeze, bang, blow'.

question: Crankshaft revolutions per complete four-stroke cycle:
explanation: the camshaft makes 1.

question: Spark ignition occurs:
explanation: so peak pressure is just after TDC.

question: Why two magnetos?

options.B: Redundancy and a faster, more complete burn

explanation: Two magnetos give redundancy and a faster, more complete burn from two flame fronts.

question: Magnetos are:
explanation: they keep working with a total electrical failure.

question: During the mag check, no RPM drop at all on one magneto suggests:

options.C: A magneto not being grounded (P-lead fault) — dangerous

explanation: No drop on a magneto means it is not being grounded — a live magneto is dangerous when hand-swinging the prop.

question: After switching to a single magneto for the check the RPM drop should:

options.D: Be within POH limits and the difference between mags within limits

explanation: typical limits ~125 rpm max drop, ~50 rpm max difference (confirm POH).

question: The carburettor:

options.D: Meters fuel into the airstream and mixes it with air

explanation: The carburettor meters fuel and mixes it with air. Mixture control adjusts the ratio; throttle controls airflow.

question: The venturi:

options.A: Creates a pressure drop that draws fuel out

explanation: The venturi's low-pressure throat draws fuel from the discharge nozzle. This pressure drop also cools the air (icing).

question: Carburettor icing can occur at outside temperatures roughly:
explanation: Carb ice can form from about −10 to +30 °C with high humidity, because fuel vaporisation and the venturi drop cool the air.

question: Carb ice is most likely at:
explanation: Carb ice is most likely at low power (descent, circuit), where throttle restriction adds to the cooling.

question: First sign of carb ice in a fixed-pitch aircraft:
explanation: A fixed-pitch prop shows carb ice as a gradual RPM drop and roughness. In a constant-speed prop, manifold pressure drops instead.

question: Carb heat applies:

options.A: Unfiltered warm air — richer mixture, less power

explanation: Carb heat sends unfiltered warm air: mixture richens and power falls. Never use it for take-off.

question: After selecting carb heat with ice present, RPM initially:

options.A: Drops further and runs rough, then recovers as ice melts

explanation: After carb heat: RPM may fall and run rough first as ice melts and passes through; then it recovers. Keep heat on.

question: When should you apply carb heat before a descent?
explanation: icing risk rises at low power.

question: Carb heat should be OFF for take-off because:

options.D: It reduces available power and is unfiltered

explanation: Carb heat off for take-off: unfiltered air and less power. You want maximum power and clean air.

question: Why lean the mixture at altitude?

options.A: Density falls, so the fixed fuel flow becomes over-rich

explanation: Air gets thinner with height, so the same fuel flow becomes rich. Leaning restores the right fuel-air ratio.

question: For take-off, landing and go-around the mixture should be:
explanation: Take-off, landing and go-around: full rich, for maximum power and cooling.

question: Detonation is:

options.D: Explosive burning of the remaining charge after normal ignition

explanation: Detonation: explosive burn of the unburned charge after normal ignition (heat/pressure/low octane/over-lean).

question: Pre-ignition is:

options.D: Burn starting before the spark, from a hot spot

explanation: Pre-ignition: burn starting before the spark, from a hot spot such as glowing carbon. Both damage the engine.

question: Detonation causes:

options.A: High CHT, roughness, possible engine damage

explanation: Detonation gives high CHT, roughness and possible piston/cylinder damage.

question: To avoid detonation you should:

options.D: Use correct fuel grade and avoid over-lean at high power

explanation: Prevent it: correct octane, rich enough at high power, good cooling.

question: Using a lower octane fuel than specified risks:
explanation: Lower octane than specified resists compression poorly → detonation. Never use car fuel or jet fuel.

question: 100LL avgas is coloured:
explanation: 100 (high-lead) was green; Jet A1 is clear/straw; never put jet fuel in a piston engine.

question: Water in fuel:

options.D: Sinks (denser) — checked at the sump drains

explanation: Water is denser than avgas, so it sinks — sump drains at the lowest points reveal it.

question: Where do you drain fuel samples?

options.C: Each tank sump and the fuel strainer

explanation: Drain every tank sump and the strainer; sump low points collect water and dirt.

question: Vapour lock is:

options.D: Fuel vaporising in lines, starving the engine

explanation: Vapour lock: fuel boils in the line, starving the engine, more likely in heat.

question: Aircraft engines are cooled mainly by:

options.D: Ram air through baffles over cylinder fins (air-cooled)

explanation: Air-cooled engines use ram air over fins guided by baffles; oil helps internally.

question: Shock cooling can result from:
explanation: cylinders cool unevenly and can crack.

question: High CHT in a climb: best action?

options.B: Enrich mixture, lower nose/increase airspeed, reduce power

explanation: High CHT: enrich the mixture, lower the nose for speed, reduce power. Never lean when hot.

question: Oil functions:

options.A: Lubricate, cool, clean, seal, protect against corrosion

explanation: Oil lubricates, cools, cleans, seals and protects against corrosion.

question: After start, no oil pressure within about 30 s (per POH):
explanation: No oil pressure within ~30 s of start → shut down; bearings can fail within seconds.

question: The C152 (Lycoming O-235) lubrication system is:
explanation: The O-235 uses a wet sump: oil is stored in the crankcase sump.

question: High oil temperature can indicate:

options.A: Low oil level, poor cooling, or friction problem

explanation: High oil temperature: low oil, poor cooling, or friction. Check oil level pre-flight.

question: Priming (cold start) is used to:

options.C: Add fuel to the cylinders for starting

explanation: over-priming risks fire on start.

question: A stationary propeller must be treated as:

options.D: Potentially live — a magneto can fire if it is moved

explanation: A stationary prop is always 'live' — a magneto can fire if it moves.

question: A fixed-pitch propeller is:

options.B: Optimised for one speed range; climb vs cruise compromise

explanation: Fixed pitch = compromise; a climb prop climbs well but cruises slower, and vice versa.

question: Fixed-pitch prop: in a dive with constant throttle RPM will:
explanation: In a dive the prop is driven faster: RPM rises. Watch the RPM limit.

question: Fixed-pitch prop: in a climb at constant throttle RPM will:
explanation: In a climb (slower airspeed, high AoA) RPM falls at constant throttle.

question: P-factor at high power/high angle of attack yaws a clockwise-rotating prop (from cockpit) aeroplane:
explanation: descending blade has greater angle of attack → more thrust on the right side → left yaw.

question: Torque reaction tends to roll a clockwise-prop aeroplane:
explanation: Torque reaction rolls the aircraft opposite to prop rotation: clockwise prop → left roll.

question: Fuel selector/shutoff on C152 is normally:
explanation: The C152 fuel valve is ON in normal operation; both tanks feed by gravity.

question: C152 fuel system:
explanation: High wing tanks feed the carburettor by gravity, so no pump is needed.

question: Alternator failure indication:
explanation: Alternator failure shows as ammeter discharge or a low-voltage warning; the battery then powers the aircraft.

question: Alternator failure action:

options.A: Reduce electrical load, monitor battery, land as soon as practical

explanation: magnetos still fire; flaps are manual on most C152 (confirm).

question: A tripped circuit breaker:

options.C: May be reset once if no smoke/smell; do not reset repeatedly

explanation: A popped breaker may be reset once if there is no smoke/smell; repeated resets risk fire.

question: Master switch controls:
explanation: ignition is separate.

question: Engine fire on start (C152 technique): continue cranking to:

options.A: Draw flames into the engine and extinguish

explanation: if it persists: mixture cut-off, fuel off, master off, evacuate.

question: Engine fire in flight (typical):

options.B: Fuel selector off, mixture cut-off, master off, land immediately

explanation: follow the POH emergency checklist.

question: Normal engine shutdown is by:

options.A: Mixture to idle cut-off, then ignition off after the prop stops

explanation: checks the mixture control and avoids afterfire.

question: Semi-monocoque structure:

options.A: Skin carries a share of load with frames/stringers

explanation: Semi-monocoque: skin carries a large share of the load with frames and stringers — strong and light.

question: Structural loads:
explanation: Five structural loads: tension, compression, shear, bending, torsion. Example: a wing spar bends under lift (tension underneath, compression on top).

question: Primary controls:
explanation: Primary controls move the aircraft about its three axes: ailerons (roll), elevator (pitch), rudder (yaw).

question: Secondary controls include:
explanation: Secondary controls (flaps, trim) modify lift/drag or reduce control forces; they are not needed for basic control.

question: Adverse yaw is caused by:

options.D: Differential drag: the down-going aileron has more drag

explanation: rudder is used to counter it.

question: The further effect of rudder is:
explanation: Further effect of rudder: roll, because the outer wing moves faster and generates more lift.

question: The further effect of aileron is:
explanation: Further effect of aileron: yaw (adverse yaw), because the down-going aileron creates more drag; use rudder to balance.

question: Elevator changes primarily:
explanation: Elevator changes pitch attitude, and therefore airspeed (attitude + power = performance).

question: Trim tab:

options.C: Relieves control force; does not change attitude by itself

explanation: Trim removes stick force, not the control need: set attitude first, then trim off the force.

question: Flaps increase:
explanation: they lower stall speed and allow a steeper approach.

question: The stall warning device:

options.D: Warns approaching the critical angle of attack

explanation: The stall warner alerts you before the critical angle of attack is reached; it is not an airspeed warning.

question: The pitot-static system feeds:
explanation: ASI (pitot + static), altimeter and VSI (static only). Check for blockages during pre-flight.

question: Blocked pitot tube (static open): the ASI behaves like:

options.A: An altimeter (reads higher in a climb)

explanation: worse in a climb, reading low in a descent; freezes in level flight.

question: Blocked static port:

options.C: Altimeter freezes, VSI reads zero, ASI errors

explanation: Blocked static: altimeter frozen, VSI zero, ASI errors. Select alternate static if fitted.

question: Alternate static source (cabin) causes:

options.D: Small error, ASI/altimeter read slightly high

explanation: Alternate static (cabin air) is lower than outside static, so ASI/altimeter read slightly high and the VSI shows a brief climb when selected.

question: Pitot heat is used:
explanation: Pitot heat is for visible moisture near freezing; not for normal dry VFR flying.

question: Attitude/heading gyro instruments are driven by:
explanation: Gyro instruments (AI, DI) are spun by vacuum or electricity. A vacuum failure shows on the suction gauge.

question: Gyroscopic rigidity means:

options.A: The gyro axis stays fixed in space

explanation: Rigidity: a spinning gyro keeps its axis fixed in space, which is why the DI holds heading.

question: Precession: a force applied to a spinning gyro acts:

options.C: 90° later in the direction of rotation

explanation: Precession: a force on a spinning gyro takes effect 90° later in the direction of rotation.

question: The turn coordinator shows:
explanation: The turn coordinator shows rate of roll/turn and the ball shows balance.

question: Ball out to the left in a right turn indicates:

options.C: Skid or slip — uncoordinated; correct with rudder

explanation: "step on the ball."

question: Nosewheel castoring/steering on the ground is via:

options.C: Rudder pedals linked to the nosewheel and brakes

explanation: Nosewheel steering is via rudder pedals (linked) plus differential braking.

question: Independent toe brakes allow:
explanation: Toe brakes let you brake one wheel to pivot in tight turns.

question: C152 landing gear:
explanation: no "gear down" check.

question: Flaps on most C150/152 are:
explanation: (confirm on your airframe).

question: CO risk in a light aircraft:

options.A: Carbon monoxide from exhaust via cabin heat

explanation: symptoms: headache, drowsiness; fresh air, land.

question: Cabin heat comes from:

options.D: Air heated by the exhaust shroud

explanation: a cracked exhaust means CO risk.

question: Load factor is:
explanation: Load factor n = lift ÷ weight. 1g in straight and level; 2g in a 60° bank.

question: In a level, coordinated 60° bank turn, load factor is:
Stall speed increases by:
explanation: Stall speed increases by √n. At 2g Vs rises ×1.41. Example: 50 kt → 71 kt at 60° bank.

question: Load factor in a 45° bank:
explanation: At 45° bank n = 1/cos45° ≈ 1.41, so Vs rises ~19%.

question: Va decreases when:
explanation: Va scales with √(weight).

question: Structural fatigue arises from:
explanation: Fatigue: repeated stress cycles start cracks that grow. Inspect regularly.

question: Corrosion is best prevented by:
explanation: Corrosion: prevent by inspection, cleaning, drainage and treatment.

question: Which surface prevents wing icing? (fixed-wing light aircraft)
explanation: Light trainers have no anti-icing: avoid icing conditions.

question: Basic Empty Mass (BEM) includes:

options.B: Airframe, engine, fixed equipment, unusable fuel, full oil

explanation: BEM includes airframe, engine, fixed equipment, unusable fuel and full oil — but not crew, fuel or baggage.

question: Take-off mass =
explanation: Take-off mass = BEM + crew + passengers + baggage + usable fuel.

question: CG is:

options.C: The point where the total weight acts

explanation: CG is where the total weight acts; the aircraft balances at that point.

question: Moment =
explanation: Moment = weight × arm (distance from datum). Sum moments ÷ sum weights = CG.

question: CG position =
explanation: CG = total moment ÷ total weight.

question: A forward CG generally causes:

options.C: Higher stall speed, more stable, heavier controls

explanation: Forward CG: stable, heavier controls, higher stall speed, more back-pressure needed to flare.

question: An aft CG generally causes:

options.C: Lower stall speed, less stable, risk of pitch instability

explanation: Aft CG: lighter controls, lower stall speed, less stability; risk of unrecoverable pitch-up/stall.

question: Maximum take-off mass is exceeded. The consequences include:

options.A: Longer take-off run, poorer climb, higher stall speed

explanation: Overweight → higher stall speed, longer take-off, weaker climb, higher structural loads.

question: Density altitude increases with:

options.C: High temperature, high altitude, high humidity

explanation: Density altitude rises with heat, height and humidity — performance falls.

Which factors *increase* take-off distance?

options.B: Higher weight, tailwind, wet/soft grass, uphill slope, higher density altitude

explanation: All these lengthen the take-off: weight, tailwind, wet/soft grass, uphill, and high density altitude. Relevant at LKBE grass.

question: A headwind on take-off:
explanation: A headwind reduces groundspeed at lift-off, shortening the run.

question: Wet grass on landing:

options.A: Reduces braking effectiveness and increases landing roll

explanation: Wet grass cuts braking, so landing roll grows.

question: Best glide speed (C152, F AIR QRH):
explanation: POH may say ~60 KIAS; fly F AIR's 65.

question: Ground effect:

options.A: Reduces induced drag near the surface (within about one wingspan)

explanation: aircraft may float on landing.

question: Stall speed with flaps extended:
explanation: Flaps increase lift, lowering stall speed.

question: Heavier aircraft — stall speed:
explanation: Heavier aircraft need more lift → higher stall speed.

question: Crosswind component = wind speed × sin(angle between wind and runway). Wind 30 kt at 40° off the runway heading:
explanation: sin 40° ≈ 0.64 → 19 kt. Headwind = cos 40° × 30 ≈ 23 kt.

question: Rule-of-thumb crosswind fractions (30°/45°/60°/90°):
explanation: Crosswind fractions of wind speed: 30° ≈ ½, 45° ≈ ⅔, 60° ≈ ⅚, 90° = all.

question: C152 demonstrated crosswind (typical):
explanation: check your POH; it is *demonstrated*, not a legal limit.

question: Range in a headwind:
explanation: A headwind lowers groundspeed, so range falls.

question: Endurance is maximised by flying at:

options.B: Minimum-power speed (slower than best range speed)

explanation: Maximum endurance = minimum power (slower than best range). Best range = higher speed.

question: True airspeed vs IAS: TAS increases roughly:
explanation: TAS ≈ CAS + 2% per 1000 ft. Example: 90 kt at 4000 ft → ≈97 kt TAS.

question: One nautical mile equals:
explanation: 1 NM = 1852 m. 1 statute mile = 1609 m.

question: One minute of latitude equals:
explanation: 1 minute of latitude = 1 NM (60 NM per degree).

question: Distance between 49°N and 50°N along a meridian ≈
A great circle:

options.B: Crosses meridians at a constant angle
options.D: Is the shortest distance between two points on the sphere

question: A rhumb line:

options.B: Crosses all meridians at the same angle

explanation: A rhumb line crosses meridians at the same angle: easy to fly, slightly longer.

question: The ICAO 1:500 000 aeronautical chart uses a:

options.D: Lambert conformal conic projection (straight line ≈ great circle)

explanation: Lambert conformal conic: straight line ≈ great circle, distances almost constant — suits VFR charts.

question: 12 cm on a 1:500 000 chart is about:
The angle between true and magnetic north is:

question: Isogonal lines join places with:
explanation: agonic line = zero variation.

question: True course 090°, variation 4°E. Magnetic course?

question: True course 270°, variation 3°W. Magnetic course?
explanation: "west is best" (add).

question: Deviation is caused by:

options.B: Magnetic influence of the aircraft itself

explanation: Deviation comes from the aircraft's own magnetic fields; it varies by heading and is on the compass card.

question: A compass swing is required after:

options.C: Engine change, lightning strike, or major electrical/avionics change

explanation: Swing the compass after an engine change, lightning strike, major electrical work or new radios.

question: ANDS: on an east/west heading, acceleration produces an apparent turn toward:
explanation: accelerate north, decelerate south.

question: UNOS: turning through north, the compass will:
explanation: overshoot when turning through south.

question: The magnetic compass is unreliable in turns primarily because of:
explanation: Magnetic dip (vertical field component) causes turning and acceleration errors.

question: The DI must be realigned with the compass about every:

options.B: 10–15 min in steady straight and level flight

explanation: Realign the DI to the compass every 10–15 min in straight and level, unaccelerated flight.

question: Apparent drift of the DI depends on:
explanation: Apparent DI drift depends on latitude (Earth rotation): maximum at the poles, zero at the equator.

question: 1 kt equals:
explanation: 1 kt = 1 NM per hour.

question: Distance per minute at 120 kt:
explanation: At 120 kt you cover 2 NM per minute.

question: Fuel flow 20 L/h. Flight time 1 h 40 min. Fuel required:

explanation: Max drift ≈ wind/TAS × 60 = 20/90 × 60 ≈ 13°.

question: 1-in-60 rule: 1° of error ≈
explanation: 1-in-60: 1° subtends ~1 NM at 60 NM (about 1 m at 60 m).

question: After 30 NM you are 3 NM right of track. Track error:

question: Which is *not* a good visual checkpoint?

options.C: Motorway crossing your track at a large angle

explanation: Choose unique, large features. Many similar villages give ambiguity.

question: Line features that cross your track at a large angle are preferred because:

options.A: They give a clear fix along the track

explanation: A crossing line feature gives a clear fix along your track; a parallel one doesn't.

question: VOR operates in the:
explanation: VOR: VHF 108.00–117.95 MHz. Line of sight only.

question: A VOR measures bearing by:

options.C: Phase difference between a reference and variable signal

explanation: VOR compares the phase of a reference signal with a rotating variable signal; the difference is the bearing.

question: Total VOR system accuracy is typically:
explanation: matches F AIR's ±5° tolerance on radio aids.

question: VOR signals are affected by:
explanation: VHF is line-of-sight: terrain shielding limits range; scalloping is a signal quality effect.

question: Above the VOR station there is a:
explanation: Directly above a VOR the signal is unreliable (cone of confusion); the needle flickers.

question: NDB/ADF operates in:
explanation: NDB uses LF/MF (~190–1750 kHz); ground wave and sky wave effects cause errors.

question: The ADF needle points:
explanation: The ADF needle points to the station, giving a relative bearing, not a radial.

question: Which is *not* an ADF error?
explanation: scalloping is a VOR effect.

question: Night effect is worst at:
explanation: Night effect worst at dawn/dusk (sky-wave interference).

question: Mountain effect on ADF is caused by:

options.D: Reflection of the signal off high terrain

explanation: Mountain effect: reflected signals cause needle errors.

question: DME measures:
explanation: DME measures slant range, not ground distance.

question: DME reads roughly 1 NM directly overhead the station at 6000 ft AGL because:
explanation: Overhead at 6000 ft AGL ≈ 1 NM because 6000 ft ≈ 1 NM slant range.

question: DME operates in:
explanation: DME uses UHF 962–1213 MHz (paired with a VOR frequency).

question: The minimum number of GNSS satellites for a 3-D position plus time is:
explanation: Four satellites: three for position plus one for time correction (3D fix).

question: GNSS altitude is used for:

options.B: Not the legal altimeter reference — use the pressure altimeter

explanation: GNSS altitude is not the legal reference; use the barometric altimeter with QNH.

question: The universal emergency VHF frequency:
explanation: 121.5 MHz is the international VHF emergency (guard) frequency.

question: ELT frequencies:
explanation: ELTs transmit on 121.5 and 406 MHz; 406 is the satellite-monitored frequency.

question: VHF communications band:
explanation: VHF comm band: 118–137 MHz. Nav band: 108–118.

question: Mode S transponder differs from Mode A/C by:
explanation: Mode S uses selective interrogation and reports more data (e.g. altitude, ID).

question: GNSS accuracy improved by SBAS such as:
explanation: EGNOS is the European SBAS improving GPS accuracy/integrity.

question: QNH gives:
explanation: QNH sets the altimeter to read altitude above mean sea level.

question: QFE gives:

question: Altitude vs height vs elevation: elevation is:

options.C: Height of the ground above MSL

explanation: Elevation = height of the ground (or a point) above MSL; altitude is aircraft above MSL; height is above a point/ground.

question: A flight level is:

options.D: Surface of constant pressure referenced to 1013.25, in hundreds of feet

explanation: Flight level = pressure surface referenced to 1013.25, in hundreds of feet (e.g. FL95 = 9500 ft).

question: 1 hPa ≈ how many feet near sea level?
explanation: 1 hPa ≈ 30 ft near sea level, 1 hPa ≈ 8 m.

question: QNH is 1003. You forget to change from 1013 to QNH. The altimeter reads:

explanation: dangerous: you are lower than indicated.

question: "High to low, look out below" means:

question: Colder-than-ISA air:

question: Pressure altitude is:

question: Density altitude is:

explanation: Density altitude = pressure altitude corrected for temperature; used for performance.

question: A stopped VSI and frozen altimeter suggest:
explanation: Frozen altimeter and stopped VSI = blocked static source.

question: Altimeter lag/instrument error is corrected by:
explanation: Instrument error/lag is minimised by calibration and awareness; fly attitude and power, not the needle.

question: True altitude above sea level differs from indicated altitude with QNH set mainly due to:

question: Dead reckoning uses:

explanation: Dead reckoning predicts position from heading, TAS, time and wind.

question: A "gross error check" is:

explanation: Gross error check: a quick sanity check (sun, coast, big landmark) that you're in roughly the right place.

question: 10° drift lines help you:

explanation: Drift lines at ±10° help judge track error/wind fast and choose corrections.

question: First action when uncertain of position:

question: Circle of uncertainty grows with:

options.C: Time since last fix and possible wind error

explanation: The circle of uncertainty grows with time since the last fix and the wind error.

question: Best strategy when lost:

options.A: Fly to a large line feature (motorway, river, railway) to convert "lost" to "on this line"

explanation: Fly to a large line feature (motorway, river, railway) — turns 'lost' into 'on this line'.

question: Ask for help (radar/DF/FIS) when:
explanation: Ask for help early; fuel and daylight shrink options later.

question: Diversion planning in flight: measure track and distance, estimate heading/GS, revise ETA and fuel, then:

options.A: Fly it while refining the plan

explanation: Diversion: measure, plan, then fly it while refining. Keep flying the aircraft first.

question: Map orientation: you should:

options.B: Keep the chart oriented to the ground, track at top

explanation: Orient the chart to the ground/track up; it reduces confusion.

question: Which errors are most common in visual navigation?

options.A: Poor lookout, lost time, over-reliance on GPS, failing to update ETA

explanation: Most errors: poor lookout, lost time, GPS over-reliance, not updating ETA/fuel.

question: A flight plan is required for:
